newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-SAMPRAS KEEPS AN EYE ON THE WEATHER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS KEEPS AN EYE ON THE WEATHER.

text.p: It is usually the British who are obsessed by the weather but world number one Pete Sampras will be scanning the daily forecasts from La Meteorologie Nationale more anxiously than anyone from now until June 8.

World number one Sampras, who beat local hope Fabrice Santoro 6-3 7-5 6-1 on Monday, confessed he was "hoping and praying" for a warm, sunny fortnight which will significantly improve his chances of winning the grand slam title he now craves above all else.

Good weather will ensure the Roland Garros courts stay quicker than normal and allow Sampras to escape from the baseline clutches of the clay specialists who will be happy for rain to return as soon as possible.

"It makes a huge difference," said Sampras. "When it rains or it's cold, it makes things a lot heavier. For my game I'm hoping and praying it stays this way. The conditions can change the whole course of a match."

Already given a timely push by the withdrawals of Andre Agassi, Boris Becker, Michael Stich, Todd Martin and Thomas Enqvist, Sampras still has to find a way past the massed ranks of Spanish clay experts, compatriot Michael Chang and the dangerous Goran Ivanisevic.
But the men's draw looks full of unpredictable names and the narrow first round escape of Thomas Muster on Monday merely strengthened the impression this will not be a straightforward tournament.
"It's anyone's year really," acknowledged Sampras. "There's not really a strong favourite here. There are a lot of dark horses who could sneak through the draw and win it."
The American himself has never been beyond the semifinals in Paris, but denies he is suffering from a mental block when it comes to playing on clay.
"This is the only grand slam tournament I haven't won so I'll do whatever I can to try and win here. I've won every other major and been number one for a while so this is the only thing left.
"You have to deal with the heat in Australia and sometimes at the U.S. Open, but the French is just tougher on the mind. It's not really tennis, it's more of a fight."
"Clay is not a surface I grew up on and I have to work a lot harder. It's the toughest event for me to win but I know I can do it."
